evaluation.positioning_hook: Kevin, a bullied teen trapped between a food obsession, a strict Christian home, and a first love, spirals toward self-destruction when his closest friend and his girlfriend each reveal their own hidden pain.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional lane is clear: teen shame, first love, family pressure, and body-image distress are all recognizable entry points. The material is more niche than broad commercial fare because it leans hard into confession and social pain rather than a clean genre engine.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The central premise emerges as Kevin’s struggle with binge eating, shame, and the people around him, and the script states that plainly. The hook is more thematic than engine-driven, so it reads as a character crisis rather than a sharply escalating feature premise.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Kevin has a visible wound and a strong internal contradiction, but much of his behavior is stated directly in dialogue and internal monologue rather than dramatized through choice. Claire and Mike add emotional texture, yet they mostly orbit Kevin’s distress instead of generating fully independent momentum.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script is willing to put eating disorder shame, Christian household pressure, queer panic, and assault trauma in the same emotional field. The execution stays close to direct statement and on-the-nose confrontation, which keeps the material from feeling as formally daring as the subject matter could support.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves in a sequence of scenes and revelations, but the forward drive is interrupted by repetition of the same emotional beats: Kevin eats, feels shame, argues, and retreats. The Act 3 material is outlined rather than dramatized, so the feature shape does not yet land with full propulsion.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A teen male binge-eating story with faith pressure and a queer-friendship thread is a fresh combination on the page. The script’s most original elements are present, but they are still presented in a familiar issue-drama mode rather than in a form that makes the premise feel inevitable and singular.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is specific in its social pressures — school, church-inflected home life, cafeteria hierarchy, and teen social media culture all show up. Still, the setting functions mostly as a container for scenes rather than a layered ecosystem with its own rules and institutions.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a raw, diary-like tone and is unafraid of blunt emotional speech. It also shifts between earnest drama, blunt comedy, and heavy trauma material in a way that feels more improvised than fully controlled.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the surface, there are deeper reserves around shame, identity, family control, sexuality, and self-worth. The draft points toward that depth directly, but it has not yet fully hidden or layered it in a way that invites a slow-burn discovery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Kevin, Jackie, Mike, and Claire create a workable emotional web, and the family-versus-friends tension gives the story shape. The relationships are strongest when they collide, but most scenes still serve Kevin’s central arc rather than generating multiple independent story engines.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Kevin is built around a painful contradiction.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a lead role an actor can really inhabit: a teen who wants love, control, and relief at the same time. Young dramatic leads and indie buyers looking for a performance-first festival title will see the part immediately.
strengths.evidence: Kevin hides his eating, cries alone, then later admits he is eating the pain away and tests himself online.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The subject matter is commercially legible.
strengths.what_it_means: Eating disorder shame, first love, and family pressure are easy to explain in one sentence, which helps the project travel to managers, buyers, and audiences quickly. This is the kind of emotional premise that can attract streamer drama buyers and festival programmers looking for a youth-facing issue story.
strengths.evidence: Kevin’s bingeing, Claire’s anorexia confession, and the Christian household conflict are all stated directly in the dialogue.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family pressure is sharply defined.
strengths.what_it_means: Jackie’s strict, religious parenting gives the story a clear home-base antagonist and a built-in emotional engine. That kind of parent-child friction is attractive to actors who like volatile domestic material and to buyers who want a contained, character-driven drama.
strengths.evidence: Jackie prays over dinner, slaps Kevin, blasts Christian music, and condemns homosexuality in the home.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Claire gives the script a second emotional lane.
strengths.what_it_means: Her anorexia backstory and romantic connection to Kevin widen the movie beyond a single-protagonist issue piece and create a teen relationship hook. That gives the project a young ensemble appeal and a clear role for a breakout actress.
strengths.evidence: Claire confesses her eating disorder, talks about being tube-fed, and later becomes Kevin’s girlfriend.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The material is built for contained production.
strengths.what_it_means: School, home, bedroom, cafeteria, and club interiors keep the budget in a producer-friendly lane without needing spectacle to carry the movie. That makes it a practical play for indie financiers and platform buyers who like contained contemporary dramas.
strengths.evidence: Most scenes take place in bedrooms, kitchens, classrooms, hallways, and a single club sequence.

whats_special.headline: This script has a clear emotional lane and a lead role with real actor appeal: a teen boy fighting shame, appetite, and family control while trying to hold onto first love. The contemporary footprint is contained, the social issue stakes are easy to communicate, and the material sits in a festival-friendly drama lane that can be packaged around performance.

lead_characters.name: Kevin
lead_characters.hook: Kevin is a sensitive, angry, self-conscious teen whose body becomes the battleground for everything he cannot say out loud. He wants affection, autonomy, and relief, but he keeps reaching for food, secrecy, and sarcasm instead, which makes him feel both vulnerable and combustible.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea — a young lead whose interior pain leaks out through silence, irritation, and sudden emotional collapse. Teen actors looking for a prestige breakout role get a part that can play shame, romance, family rebellion, and self-destruction in one turn.

lead_characters.name: Claire
lead_characters.hook: Claire is the cool, music-loving girl who looks self-possessed on the surface but carries her own history of body control and medical trauma. She is affectionate, blunt, and emotionally direct, which makes her feel like both a romantic escape and a mirror for Kevin’s pain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Kaitlyn Dever had in Short Term 12 — emotionally open, quietly wounded, and able to turn a conversation into a full character reveal. Young actresses chasing a breakout indie part will want the chance to play warmth, honesty, and damage without losing charm.

lead_characters.name: Mike
lead_characters.hook: Mike is Kevin’s closest friend, the one person who can joke with him, challenge him, and still sit beside him when the room gets heavy. He reads as observant and emotionally porous, with a private life that the script begins to open into something darker and more complicated.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This has the emotional-support-to-trauma pivot space of a supporting lead in The Perks of Being a Wallflower, where the role starts as the best friend and expands into the story’s emotional conscience. A young actor who wants a part with tenderness, humor, and a later dramatic turn will see the opportunity immediately.

lead_characters.name: Jackie
lead_characters.hook: Jackie is Kevin’s mother, a strict, religious, controlling presence who believes discipline is love and shame is correction. She is not written as a soft parent; she is a force of doctrine, habit, and fear, which gives the home scenes their pressure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Viola Davis had in Fences — a parent whose love is inseparable from force, judgment, and survival logic. Character actresses who like playing moral authority with emotional volatility will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.hook: David is Claire’s father, a protective adult who can shift from polite host to hard boundary in a single beat. He functions as the household authority and the person who makes the romance feel socially real, not just teen fantasy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the grounded-parent territory of Jeffrey Wright in a domestic drama — a role that can turn a dinner-table scene into a power scene with very little screen time. Strong character actors who like efficient authority roles will see the value.

lead_characters.name: Lily
lead_characters.hook: Lily is Claire’s mother, the warmer counterweight to David and the adult who tries to keep the house emotionally livable. She has a practical, protective energy and gives the family scenes a softer register.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded domestic texture of Patricia Clarkson in a family drama — not the center of the movie, but the person who makes the home feel inhabited. Character actresses who specialize in warmth with edge will know how to play it.

lead_characters.name: Ben
lead_characters.hook: Ben is one of the school bullies, loud and performative, using body-shaming as social currency. He is less a full person than a pressure source, but he helps define the social cruelty around Kevin.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of high-school antagonist role that lets a young actor play swagger and menace in a compact package, similar to the bully energy in Eighth Grade. Emerging teen actors often use parts like this to make a sharp impression fast.

lead_characters.name: Stephanie
lead_characters.hook: Stephanie is Ben’s partner in cruelty, quick to mock Kevin and quick to escalate the social humiliation. She functions as a sharp, judgmental peer presence in the school ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the mean-girl lane that can be played with the brittle precision of Mean Girls supporting roles — a part that gives a young actress a clear social function and a few memorable lines. It is the kind of role casting directors use to populate a teen ensemble with attitude.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Williams
lead_characters.hook: Ms. Williams is the school authority figure who moves quickly from discipline to escalation. She represents institutional control rather than emotional understanding, which keeps the school scenes tense.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sharp, no-nonsense educator role that can play like the adult authority in Election — efficient, judgmental, and scene-stealing in small doses. Strong character actors who can make bureaucracy feel personal will fit it well.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Platty
lead_characters.hook: Ms. Platty is the ISS monitor, a small but functional authority presence who keeps the school world moving. She is more texture than arc, but she helps widen the institutional feel of the setting.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact authority role that gives a character actor a clean, memorable beat, similar to the school-adult texture in The Wire or Eighth Grade. It is useful casting for performers who can make one scene feel specific.

lead_characters.name: Mr. Jones
lead_characters.hook: Mr. Jones is the classroom teacher who delivers the semester warning and grades Kevin in a way that immediately establishes academic pressure. He is part of the system that keeps Kevin feeling behind.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic grounded-teacher role in the lane of a small but memorable adult part from Dead Poets Society or Election. Working character actors often like these roles because they establish stakes with very little screen time.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a raw, performance-first teen drama with real emotional bruises.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors coming out of shorts or microbudget dramas, especially those who already work in intimate, actor-centered storytelling. The material rewards close framing, naturalistic dialogue, and the ability to hold uncomfortable emotional space without needing spectacle.
director_appeal.detail: The movie lives or dies on performance, tone control, and the ability to make domestic scenes feel charged. That makes it attractive to directors who want a contained contemporary feature that can travel on cast work and emotional honesty.

buyer_appeal.lane: Festival drama / prestige indie / streamer acquisition lane
buyer_appeal.detail: The contained school-and-home footprint means a buyer can package this around a strong young lead and a credible director without needing expensive set pieces. The eating-disorder, first-love, and family-pressure mix gives it a clear festival-to-platform path and a youth-adjacent audience hook.

considerations.detail: The final section reads as a roadmap for what happens next rather than a fully staged climax. One primary lever would be to choose the single emotional collision that ends the movie and build the last act around that sequence so the feature lands with a completed dramatic shape.

considerations.area: Kevin’s inner life is often stated directly.
considerations.detail: A lot of the emotional truth arrives in monologue, mind-voice, or characters explaining what they feel. A next pass could let one or two of those admissions arrive through behavior or conflict first, which would give the same pain more cinematic force.

considerations.area: The same shame beat returns several times.
considerations.detail: Kevin eats, feels bad, argues, and retreats in multiple scenes, which establishes the pattern clearly. The version of the script where one of those repetitions turns into a new choice — not just a new confession — would sharpen escalation and keep the middle moving forward.

considerations.area: The music references are clearance items.
considerations.detail: Metallica, Korn, Freddie Dredd, Nirvana, and AC/DC are all named on the page. If those songs or recordings become story-critical in production, they should be cleared early or swapped for original placeholders.

considerations.area: The club sequence can stay compact.
considerations.detail: The party material currently introduces several named friends in a short stretch. One simplification lever would be to fold a couple of those roles together so the social world stays vivid without expanding the cast footprint.
